messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam was seventeen when a routine sore throat turned into sepsis, landing him in the ICU for three weeks. He remembered the first spinal tap—the needle sliding between his vertebrae, the antiseptic smell that filled his nostrils, the way his body had betrayed him overnight. He recovered physically, but something had lodged itself deep. Now, at nineteen, he worked as a peer counselor at a community youth center, a job that once gave him purpose. But lately, every session felt like walking a minefield.

The triggers were everywhere. A client mentioned having an IV, and Liam’s chest tightened—his heart hammering, palms slick. That smell of hospital disinfectant, even diluted in hand sanitizer, made his stomach drop. He had come to believe his body was now an enemy, something that could turn on him without warning. When a colleague moved too quickly to grab a file, Liam flinched so hard he nearly knocked over his chair. The physical reactivity—the racing pulse, the dizziness—only reinforced that his body was unreliable. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; he was just going through the motions.

Liam developed strategies to cope, but they looped back on him. He avoided anything discussed in therapy—if a client brought up medical trauma, he’d steer the conversation elsewhere, or cut the session short. He started staying up until two or three in the morning, delaying sleep because he knew the nightmares would come. When his girlfriend reached for him in the dark, he’d startle, and that only made her more hesitant. He also avoided hospitals, ambulances, even routine physical exams—he hadn’t seen a doctor in over a year. Each time he smelled antiseptic, he felt the old terror surge, and in response he’d leave the room or change the subject. That momentary relief came at a cost: the avoidance kept his belief that his body was a threat firmly in place.

His girlfriend, worried, asked why he couldn’t sleep. Liam told her his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. That conviction—that his body was forever broken—made hospital smells, needles, and procedures even more potent triggers. Every time he felt that startle response to an unexpected movement, he scanned the environment for more signs of danger, which made him more attuned to hospital-like cues. The threat itself drove his maladaptive strategies: to avoid the racing heart, he delayed sleep; to avoid the startle, he stayed home; but sleep deprivation only worsened his physical reactivity.

Last week, a youth center visitor wore a hospital wristband from a recent visit. Liam saw it and felt his chest seize, then excused himself to the bathroom, where he nearly vomited. That evening, he ignored his girlfriend’s texts and stayed up until dawn, scrolling aimlessly. She finally told him he needed to talk to someone. What frightened Liam most was the idea that if he couldn’t handle a wristband, how could he ever be a counselor again? But he was also tired of living on guard. He came to the clinic hoping, against his own doubts, that he might one day trust his body enough to let himself sleep.
